name: Progressive Encephalomyelitis with Rigidity and Myoclonus (PERM)

clinicalPearls: A severe variant at the extreme end of the stiff-person spectrum, combining axial and limb rigidity with brainstem, autonomic and long-tract involvement.
Presents subacutely with painful muscle stiffness and spasms, prominent stimulus-sensitive and spontaneous myoclonus, and exaggerated startle.
Brainstem features distinguish it from classic stiff-person syndrome: ophthalmoplegia, nystagmus, dysarthria, dysphagia and gaze palsies.
Dysautonomia is common and potentially fatal, with labile blood pressure, arrhythmia, hyperhidrosis and thermoregulatory instability.
Most cases are associated with glycine receptor antibodies; a subset carry anti-GAD or amphiphysin antibodies, the latter flagging paraneoplastic disease.
A paraneoplastic search is essential, particularly for breast carcinoma, thymoma, lymphoma and small cell lung cancer.
Electromyography shows continuous motor unit activity with co-contraction of agonists and antagonists, and startle studies show exaggerated responses.
Immunotherapy often produces marked improvement, contrasting with the historically poor outcome of untreated disease, so early recognition is vital.
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus is an autoimmune disorder of central nervous system inhibitory neurotransmission affecting the spinal cord and brainstem. In the majority of patients, antibodies target the alpha-1 subunit of the glycine receptor, a key inhibitory receptor concentrated in spinal and brainstem interneurons; a further group harbour antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme synthesising the inhibitory transmitter GABA, and a smaller paraneoplastic group carry amphiphysin antibodies. Loss of glycinergic and GABAergic inhibition removes the normal restraint on alpha motor neurons and interneuronal circuits, producing continuous involuntary firing that manifests as simultaneous co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles, giving the characteristic rigidity, superimposed painful spasms, myoclonus and pathologically enhanced startle. Because the brainstem is involved, cranial nerve nuclei and central autonomic pathways are also affected, accounting for oculomotor disturbance, bulbar dysfunction and the dangerous dysautonomia. Pathologically there is perivascular lymphocytic inflammation and neuronal loss in the grey matter of the cord and brainstem. The glycine receptor antibodies are considered directly pathogenic and their frequent responsiveness to immunotherapy, together with paraneoplastic associations in a proportion of cases, firmly establishes the disorder as antibody-mediated autoimmunity.
additionalDifferentials: Classic stiff-person syndrome and its focal variants
Neuromyotonia and other peripheral hyperexcitability syndromes
Serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Brainstem encephalitis of other autoimmune or infective cause
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid glycine receptor, anti-GAD and amphiphysin antibody testing
Electromyography demonstrating continuous motor unit activity and agonist-antagonist co-contraction
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands and inflammatory markers
Whole-body cross-sectional imaging and tumour markers to screen for underlying malignancy
Brain and spinal cord MRI to identify inflammatory change and exclude structural mimics
Startle reflex and exaggerated acoustic startle neurophysiology studies
Autonomic function testing where dysautonomia is suspected
redFlags: Autonomic instability with labile blood pressure or cardiac arrhythmia
Laryngospasm, bulbar dysfunction or respiratory muscle involvement threatening the airway
Features suggesting an underlying tumour such as weight loss or a palpable mass
Reduced consciousness or seizures indicating widespread encephalitis
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease historically progressed to severe disability or death, but early and sustained immunotherapy frequently yields substantial recovery. Prognosis is worse when dysautonomia is severe or when an underlying malignancy is not identified and treated.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the condition as tetanus or a functional disorder and delaying immunotherapy
Failing to test for glycine receptor antibodies when only anti-GAD is considered
Overlooking an occult tumour and thereby missing a paraneoplastic driver
Underestimating life-threatening dysautonomia and respiratory compromise
Attributing rigidity solely to a primary movement disorder and omitting antibody testing
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology (standard reference)
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice (standard reference)
management: First-line immunotherapy with corticosteroids combined with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange to remove pathogenic glycine-receptor and related antibodies
Escalation to second-line immunosuppression such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide in refractory or relapsing disease
Symptomatic control of rigidity, spasms and myoclonus with GABAergic agents such as benzodiazepines and baclofen

Detect and treat life-threatening dysautonomia in a high-dependency or critical care setting, with cardiac rhythm, blood pressure and temperature monitoring and ventilatory and swallowing support as needed
Screen for and treat an underlying malignancy, particularly breast carcinoma, thymoma, lymphoma and small cell lung cancer, especially with amphiphysin antibodies
Multidisciplinary neurology and immunology care with rehabilitation, physiotherapy and long-term relapse surveillance
